introduction: Today we begin Holy Week. We welcome Jesus into Jerusalem with palm branches and the crowd's hosanna, and a few moments later we hear the account of his Passion according to Mark. The servant in Isaiah sets his face like a flint; Paul sings of Christ who emptied himself and became obedient to death on a cross. Let us walk with the Lord this week, from the joy of his entry to the silence of the tomb, and on to Easter.

prayerOfTheFaithful.invitation: Brothers and sisters, Christ humbled himself for us and became obedient to death. Let us pray to the Father, who exalted him.
intentions: For the Church as she enters Holy Week: that she may follow her Lord with faith and love, from the palms to the cross to the empty tomb. Let us pray to the Lord.
For the people of Jerusalem and the Holy Land, and for all places torn by violence: that the King who came in peace may bring peace to the nations. Let us pray to the Lord.
For all who suffer unjustly, who are mocked, abandoned or condemned: that they may find in Christ a companion in their pain. Let us pray to the Lord.
For those who have drifted from the faith: that this week may draw them back to the Lord who never stops loving them. Let us pray to the Lord.
For ourselves: that we may keep watch with Jesus this week and take part in the liturgies of the Triduum. Let us pray to the Lord.
prayerOfTheFaithful.conclusion: Almighty Father, your Son entered Jerusalem to give his life for us. Help us to follow him faithfully this week, to share in his Passion and to rise with him at Easter. Through Christ our Lord.

reflection.title: Couldn't you watch one hour?
reflection.body:
Holy Week opens with two contrasting scenes. First, the joy of the procession: Jesus rides into Jerusalem on a young donkey, people spread their cloaks and branches on the road, and they cry out, "Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord!" Then, at the same Mass, the long reading of the Passion. The same city that welcomes him will reject him within days.

The servant in Isaiah already knew this path. He gave his back to those who struck him, "Therefore I have set my face like a flint, and I know that I won't be disappointed." Paul's hymn describes the whole mystery: Christ "emptied himself, taking the form of a servant," and "he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross."

Mark tells the Passion with few words and great honesty. A woman pours precious ointment over Jesus' head, and when others complain, he defends her: "She has done what she could." In Gethsemane, Jesus is "greatly troubled and distressed" and prays, "Abba, Father, all things are possible to you. Please remove this cup from me. However, not what I desire, but what you desire." He returns to find his friends asleep: "Couldn't you watch one hour?"

One by one, everyone leaves him. Peter denies him, and when the rooster crows, "he wept." On the cross Jesus prays the opening words of Psalm 22: "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" And at the moment of his death, it is a Roman centurion who sees the truth: "Truly this man was the Son of God!"

This week, Jesus asks us what he asked his disciples: to stay with him. Make time for the liturgies of Holy Thursday, Good Friday and the Easter Vigil if you can. Take your palm home and place it near a crucifix. And when you look at it, give him your hour.
